questions.q: Why can you successfully call a function declaration from code written above its own declaration, but not a function expression the same way?
options: Function expressions don't exist in JavaScript
Function declarations are hoisted and available throughout their scope; function expressions aren't assigned until their line actually runs
There is no real difference - both work identically
Function declarations run slower, which is why they need extra time
questions.explain: Hoisting makes a declared function available before its line executes. A function expression's variable exists early, but holds undefined until the assignment line runs.

questions.q:
What does this one-line arrow function return when called as `double(4)`?

const double = (n) => n * 2;
questions.explain: A one-line arrow function without braces implicitly returns the expression's result: 4 * 2 is 8.

options: "INC001", because arrow functions always use the object that calls them
undefined (or an error), because an arrow function has no this of its own - it uses whatever this was in scope where it was defined, not the ticket object
questions.explain: Arrow functions don't bind their own this; they inherit this from the surrounding scope at definition time, which here is not the ticket object.

questions.q: What is a parameter in a function definition?
options: A named placeholder that receives whatever value is passed in when the function is called
The value returned at the end of the function
A global variable the function can never access
questions.explain: A parameter is the named placeholder in the function's definition; the actual value supplied at call time is called the argument.
